p: The future apostle to the Gentiles first appears as the church's enemy, approving Stephen's death.
b: The verb syneudokeō means "approve, give full consent." Paul uses the same word of himself when he retells the story in 22:20. His letters never hide this past: "I persecuted the church of God" (1 Corinthians 15:9; Galatians 1:13; Philippians 3:6). Luke sets the scene so that Stephen's death and Saul's career are tied together. A saying attributed to Augustine puts it this way: if Stephen had not prayed (7:60), the church would not have had Paul.

t: Why were the apostles left alone?
p: All fled but the apostles. Many think the attack fell hardest on Stephen's Greek-speaking circle.
b: "Everyone" is a round number: a church still meets in Jerusalem later (8:3; 9:26). Why could the Twelve stay? One view (Hengel, Haenchen, many since): the attack fell mainly on the Hellenists, the Greek-speaking Jewish believers around Stephen and the Seven (6:1–6), whose criticism of the temple (6:13–14) angered the authorities, while the Aramaic-speaking apostles still worshiped in the temple. Another view: the apostles stayed on purpose, as leaders who would not abandon the city, and Luke's point is that Jerusalem remains the center (8:14). Either way, the scattering fulfills the outline of 1:8: the word now moves into "Judea and Samaria."

a: raised a loud lament over him
t: Mourning a man the court had condemned
p: Loud public mourning for someone executed by a Jewish court went against custom. The burial was a brave act.
b: Kopetos means loud lamenting with beating of the breast. The Mishnah, written down about AD 200 but reflecting older practice, says that relatives of a man executed by the court "did not lament, but they grieved, for grief is in the heart alone" (Mishnah Sanhedrin 6:6). If something like this rule held in Stephen's day, the "devout men" who buried him and wailed over him were openly saying he died unjustly. Luke uses "devout" (eulabeis) of pious Jews (2:5; Luke 2:25), so these may have been Jews who were not believers, like the Pharisee Gamaliel who had urged restraint (5:34–39).

p: The Greek verb is used of wild animals tearing their prey. Luke paints Saul as a beast loose among the flock.
b: Lymainomai means to ravage or wreck, and in Greek writers it is used of wild animals savaging something. The Greek Old Testament uses it of the wild boar that tears up God's vineyard (Psalm 80:13, Psalm 79:14 in the Greek numbering). The picture fits Paul's own memory of himself as one who tried to "destroy" the church (Galatians 1:13) and Jesus' warning about wolves among the sheep (Luke 10:3; compare Acts 20:29). "Into one house after another": the church met in homes (2:46; 5:42), so Saul raided the places where believers gathered.

a: telling the good news of the word
p: The plan of 1:8 moves forward through suffering: those driven out of Jerusalem carry the message with them.
b: Luke repeats this sentence almost word for word at 11:19, where the scattered believers reach Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch. The pattern runs through Acts: opposition does not stop the word but pushes it outward. "The word" (ho logos) is Luke's shorthand for the message about Jesus, and his summaries report its growth as if it were alive (6:7; 12:24; 19:20). Tertullian's later saying, that the blood of Christians is seed (Apology 50), puts the same idea in a slogan.

p: Not Philip the apostle but Philip of the Seven (6:5), later called "the evangelist," who settled at Caesarea.
b: Luke means the Philip named second among the Seven chosen to serve the widows (6:5). He reappears twenty years later at Caesarea as "Philip the evangelist," with four unmarried daughters who prophesied (21:8–9); this chapter ends with him arriving there (8:40). Early writers sometimes merged him with Philip the apostle (John 1:43–46): Eusebius, quoting Papias and Polycrates, speaks of "Philip" and his prophesying daughters at Hierapolis in Asia, and it is unclear which Philip is meant (Church History 3.31; 3.39). One of the Seven, chosen to serve tables, here does the work of an apostle.

p: Samaritans did not expect a son of David. They looked for the Taheb, a prophet like Moses.
b: The Samaritans kept only the five books of Moses, so the promises to David's house were not part of their hope. Later Samaritan sources speak of the Taheb, "the one who returns" or "restores," a prophet like Moses based on Deuteronomy 18:15: "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers" (Deuteronomy 18:15). The Samaritan woman's expectation of the Messiah in John 4:25 shows that the hope could be put in Jewish terms. Peter in 3:22 already presents Jesus as that prophet. For Jews of Luke's day, preaching to Samaritans was itself striking: the two peoples had quarreled for centuries over Gerizim and Jerusalem (John 4:9, 20).

p: Exorcisms and healings mark Philip as carrying on Jesus' work, as the apostles and Stephen had done.
b: Luke tells the church's story as a continuation of Jesus' own: Jesus healed the paralyzed and lame and drove out unclean spirits who shrieked (Luke 4:33–36; 5:17–26), the apostles did signs (2:43; 5:12), Stephen did great wonders and signs (6:8), and now Philip does the same in Samaria. Isaiah 35:6, where the lame leap, was read as a sign of God's coming rule. The point is not that Philip is a wonder-worker like Simon (8:9–11) but that the signs point away from him to "the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ" (8:12).

p: Second-century writers made Simon the father of all heresies. Most of their stories go far beyond Acts.
b: Justin Martyr, himself from Samaria, says Simon came from the village of Gitta, was honored as a god at Rome under Claudius, and traveled with a woman named Helena (First Apology 26). Justin saw a statue inscribed "to Simon the holy god"; an inscription found on the Tiber island in 1574 reads "to Semo Sancus," a Sabine god, and many think Justin misread it. Irenaeus calls Simon the source of all heresies and describes a Gnostic sect of Simonians (Against Heresies 1.23). The Acts of Peter has Simon fly over Rome and fall when Peter prays. These are later legends; Acts says only that Simon believed, was baptized, and was rebuked.

p: Simon is called a practitioner of mageia, the arts of the magi. The same word family names the magi of Matthew 2.
b: Mageuō comes from magos, at first a Persian priest-astrologer, then anyone who worked spells, cures, curses and wonders for pay. In Matthew 2 the magi are honored seekers; in Acts the word is negative, as with Bar-Jesus the magos on Cyprus (13:6–8) and the magic books burned at Ephesus (19:19). Magic was everywhere in the Roman world: spells for love, health and revenge survive by the thousands in the Greek magical papyri. Acts keeps drawing a line between the power of God, which cannot be bought or controlled, and magic, which tries to manage the spirit world for one's own ends.

p: The crowd gives Simon a divine title. Scholars debate whether it means he claimed to be God or an angelic power.
b: "Power" was a reverent way to name God himself (Jesus says "the right hand of the Power," Mark 14:62) and also a word for heavenly beings under God. Some think the Samaritans called their supreme God "the Great Power" and hailed Simon as his appearance on earth; Irenaeus says the Simonians later taught that Simon was the highest God. Others think he was only claimed as a power sent from God, a kind of angel. Either way Luke sets two "powers" side by side: the crowds call Simon "the Power of God," but the real "acts of power" (8:13, dynameis) come through Philip and astound Simon himself.

p: Luke uses the same two verbs three times each, so the reader sees the crowd's attention move from Simon to Philip.
b: "Listen closely" (prosechō) appears in 8:6, 10 and 11: first the crowds attend to Philip, then Luke flashes back to how they used to attend to Simon. "Astound" (existēmi) appears in 8:9, 11 and 13: Simon used to astound the people, and now he himself is astounded at what happens through Philip. The Plain keeps the same English words so the turn is visible. The magician becomes the audience.

a: the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ
p: Acts begins and ends with the kingdom of God (1:3; 28:31); here it is joined to "the name of Jesus Christ."
b: Jesus spent forty days speaking of the kingdom of God (1:3), and Paul is still proclaiming it at the end (28:23, 31). In Acts the kingdom is never preached apart from Jesus: God's rule has come near in him, and his "name" stands for his person and authority, the name into which people are baptized (8:16) and on which they call (9:14). For Samaritans, who were waiting for a Moses-like restorer, the kingdom meant the renewal of Israel's worship and life, now offered to them as well.

p: Simon believed and was baptized, then tried to buy the Spirit. What was his faith worth?
b: A false faith: many fathers and Reformers, among them Calvin, held that Simon's faith was a show or a mere admiration of miracles; he believed the signs, not the message (compare John 2:23–25). A real but untaught faith: others note that Luke uses the same words for Simon as for the Samaritans (8:12) and that Peter calls him to repent, not to be converted from scratch, so he was a true but badly confused believer. The question became a test case in arguments about whether true believers can fall away (see the topic perseverance). Luke leaves Simon's end open (8:24).

a: they sent Peter and John to them
p: John once wanted fire to fall on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:54). Now he prays for Samaritans.
b: Peter and John work as a pair in Acts 3–4, as Jesus had sent disciples out two by two (Luke 10:1). In Luke's Gospel James and John asked Jesus, "Lord, do you want us to call fire down from heaven to destroy them?" when a Samaritan village refused him (Luke 9:52–55). Luke does not point out the irony, but readers of both volumes can hardly miss it: the fire that comes down on Samaritans now is the Holy Spirit. The Jerusalem apostles also check and confirm new work, as they later do at Antioch (11:22) and in chapter 15.

a: Up to then the Spirit had fallen on none of them
t: Why did the Samaritans receive the Spirit later?
p: Baptized believers wait for the Spirit. Readers explain the gap in four different ways.
b: Unity: God held back the Spirit until apostles from Jerusalem came, so that the Samaritans, long split from the Jews, would not form a separate church (Lampe, Bruce). Faulty faith: the Samaritans' first response was enthusiasm for Philip's signs, like Simon's, and only later became real (James Dunn, 1970). A second gift: in Luke's writings the Spirit is chiefly power for witness, which can come after conversion; Pentecostal teaching builds its doctrine of baptism in the Spirit as a later experience on this passage and 19:1–7 (Stronstad). Confirmation: Catholic and Orthodox teaching sees here the rite in which the apostles' successors complete baptism (see the card on this chapter). Luke himself says only that it had not yet happened.

a: baptism into the name of the Lord Jesus
p: "Into the name" may mean being handed over to Jesus as his own. It does not settle what words were said at baptism.
b: Eis to onoma, "into the name," was used in Greek business papers of money paid into someone's account, and in Jewish usage "for the sake of" someone. Baptism "into the name of the Lord Jesus" marks the person as belonging to Jesus. Acts also says "in" or "upon" the name of Jesus Christ (2:38; 10:48), while Matthew 28:19 gives the threefold name, "into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). Most churches think Acts describes whose baptism it was, not the exact formula; Oneness Pentecostals hold that baptism must be spoken in Jesus' name only. See the card at 2:38.
orig: εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ (eis to onoma tou kyriou Iēsou)

a: began to lay their hands on them
p: An old gesture of blessing and appointing. In Acts it goes with healing, sending and the Spirit.
b: Jacob laid hands on Joseph's sons to bless them (Genesis 48:14); Moses laid hands on Joshua, who was then "full of the spirit of wisdom" (Numbers 27:18–23; Deuteronomy 34:9); worshipers laid a hand on an animal they offered (Leviticus 1:4). In Acts the apostles lay hands on the Seven (6:6), Ananias on Saul (9:17), the church at Antioch on Barnabas and Saul (13:3), and Paul on the Ephesian disciples (19:6). Hebrews counts "laying on of hands" among the basic teachings (Hebrews 6:2). The verb is in a tense that suggests the apostles went from person to person.

p: Simon's offer gave the church a word: simony, the buying or selling of spiritual office or power.
b: The early church took Simon's request as a warning about money and ministry. The Council of Chalcedon (AD 451), in its second canon, forbade any bishop to ordain for payment. In the Middle Ages "simony," the buying of church offices, became a major scandal and a target of reformers from Gregory VII to the Protestant Reformers. Dante put the simoniac popes upside down in holes in the eighth circle of hell (Inferno, canto 19), which opens with a curse on "Simon Magus." In the story itself Simon wants the authority to give the Spirit (8:19), probably to add it to his trade as a wonder-worker.

a: May your silver go to ruin, and you with it
p: Peter's words are a real curse, not a mild rebuke: "to destruction with your money and with you."
b: The Greek is an optative of wishing: "your silver, with you, be for destruction." Apōleia is the word for final ruin (Matthew 7:13; Philippians 3:19). Like the deaths of Ananias and Sapphira over money (5:1–11), the story shows how seriously Luke takes greed in the church. "God's gift" (dōrea) is Luke's term for the Spirit himself (2:38; 10:45; 11:17): what is given freely cannot be bought. Peter immediately adds a way out (8:22), so the curse works like a prophet's warning that can be turned aside by repentance.
orig: Τὸ ἀργύριόν σου σὺν σοὶ εἴη εἰς ἀπώλειαν (to argyrion sou syn soi eiē eis apōleian)

a: You have no portion or lot in this matter
p: Peter speaks in Old Testament terms: Simon has no share in this, like one cut off from the land.
b: "Portion" (meris) and "lot" (klēros) were the words for a family's allotted share of the promised land. The Levites, who served God, had none: "he has no share or inheritance with you" (Deuteronomy 12:12). Here the share is in "this matter" (logos), which can also mean "this word": the message and its gift. "Your heart is not straight with God" echoes Psalm 78:37, which says of Israel in the wilderness, "Their hearts were not firm with him" (Psalm 78:37); the Greek of that psalm uses the same word, "straight."

p: The KJV's "gall of bitterness" and "bond of iniquity" echo two Old Testament verses in Greek.
b: Gall (cholē) was bile, and in the Bible a word for poison. Deuteronomy warns, "Take care that no root is here among you that bears poison and wormwood" (Deuteronomy 29:18), a root of turning to other gods; Hebrews 12:15 uses the same image of a "root of bitterness." "The bond of wrongdoing" (syndesmos adikias) is the phrase of Isaiah 58:6 in the Greek, where God's chosen fast is "to unlock the fetters of wickedness" (Isaiah 58:6). Peter may mean that Simon is headed for bitterness, or already in it; the Greek "into" allows both.
orig: εἰς χολὴν πικρίας καὶ σύνδεσμον ἀδικίας (eis cholēn pikrias kai syndesmon adikias)

a: Pray for me yourselves, to the Lord
p: Simon asks for prayer, but only to escape punishment. Luke leaves it there; one ancient text adds that he wept.
b: Peter told Simon to pray (8:22); Simon asks the apostles to pray for him instead, and only that "none of what you have said" will happen. Some readers see the start of real repentance, others only fear. Codex Bezae and a few Western witnesses add that Simon "did not stop weeping much" (reported by Metzger), a scribe's attempt to soften the ending. Later writers, from Justin and Irenaeus on, remembered Simon as an arch-heretic and never as a penitent, but that judgment comes from the legends (see the note on 8:9), not from Acts.

p: The phrase can mean "southward" or "at midday." Travelers avoided the noon heat, so the second makes the order stranger.
b: Kata mesēmbrian literally means "at midday." In the Greek Old Testament it often means "toward the south," the direction of the midday sun, and most translations take it that way here, since the road runs southwest from Jerusalem. But in 22:6, its only other New Testament use, it plainly means "about noon." If Luke means time, the angel sends Philip out at the hottest hour onto a road through empty country, with no reason given: obedience before explanation. Both readings are possible.

t: Which is deserted, the road or Gaza?
p: The note may describe the road, or old Gaza, destroyed by a Jewish king about 96 BC and rebuilt nearer the sea.
b: Gaza was the last town before the desert road to Egypt. The Hasmonean king Alexander Jannaeus destroyed it about 96 BC (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 13.358–364); a new Gaza was later built nearer the coast, and some ancient geographers spoke of the old site as deserted. So "It is deserted" may tell the reader which road to picture, the one through empty country, or which Gaza, the abandoned one. Some scholars read it as Luke's own comment, others as part of the angel's words. The Plain leaves it outside the quotation and keeps the ambiguity.

p: Greek "Ethiopia" meant the kingdom of Kush on the upper Nile (in modern Sudan), ruled from Meroë, not modern Ethiopia.
b: For Greeks and Romans, Ethiopians were the dark-skinned peoples south of Egypt, and the name covered the kingdom of Kush with its capital at Meroë. Homer called them the "furthest of men," and for Luke's readers a man from Ethiopia came from the ends of the earth (1:8). The Hebrew Bible's Cush is the same land. Psalm 68 hoped that "Cush will run to stretch out its hands to God" (Psalm 68:31), and Zephaniah spoke of worshipers "from beyond the rivers of Cush" (Zephaniah 3:10). This man is the first fruits of that hope. Black Christians have long seen in him a sign that Africa was part of the church from the start.

t: A eunuch at the edge of the assembly
p: Deuteronomy 23:1 barred eunuchs from the assembly; Isaiah 56 promised them a name.
b: Eunouchos means a castrated man; kings used such men as trusted officials, and the word could also mean simply "court official," as the Hebrew saris does for Potiphar, who had a wife (Genesis 39:1). Luke calls him a eunuch five times, so he means it literally. The Law said, "No man whose testicles are crushed or whose penis is cut off may enter the assembly of the LORD" (Deuteronomy 23:1). Isaiah answered with a promise to faithful eunuchs: "in my house and inside my walls / I will set up for them a marker and a name / that is better than sons and daughters" (Isaiah 56:5). The man is reading Isaiah, only three chapters before that promise.
r: Deuteronomy 23:1; Isaiah 56:3–5; Genesis 39:1; Esther 1:10; Jeremiah 38:7; Matthew 19:12

p: Kandake was not a name but a royal title in Kush, used for the queen or queen mother who wielded real power.
b: The Meroitic word kandake (older spelling "Candace") was the title of the ruling queens and queen mothers of Kush. Pliny the Elder says the title had passed from queen to queen for many years (Natural History 6.186), and Strabo tells of a one-eyed Kandake who fought the Romans on Egypt's southern border about 25–21 BC (Geography 17.1.54). Royal pyramids of several such queens still stand at Meroë. So the eunuch was a finance minister of a real African kingdom. Luke's "over all her treasure" uses gaza, a Persian word for treasure, which happens to sound like the road's goal, Gaza.

a: He had come to Jerusalem to worship
p: Luke does not say whether the eunuch was a Jew, a convert to Judaism or a Gentile who worshiped Israel's God.
b: A Jew from the far south is possible: there were Jewish communities up the Nile, such as the garrison at Elephantine. A full convert is unlikely, since a eunuch could not be circumcised into the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:1). Many therefore think he was a Gentile who worshiped Israel's God, like Cornelius (10:2). But Luke presents Cornelius as the first Gentile convert (10–11; 15:7), so others think Luke saw the eunuch as a Jew or proselyte, or simply as an outsider whose standing is left unclear. Either way he had traveled perhaps 1,200 miles to worship at a temple whose inner courts he could not enter.

p: A private copy of Isaiah was an expensive possession. He read it in Greek, aloud, as ancient readers did.
b: Owning a scroll of Isaiah, perhaps 7 meters long, marked wealth and devotion. The words he reads (8:32–33) follow the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament made before Jesus, so he read Greek. "Chariot" (harma) here was probably a traveling carriage, slow enough for a man on foot to run beside it. Philip "heard him reading" (8:30) because most people read aloud; silent reading was uncommon enough that Augustine remarked on Ambrose doing it (Confessions 6.3).

a: Do you really know what you are reading?
p: Philip's question is a pun in Greek: ginōskeis ha anaginōskeis, "do you know what you are reading?"
b: The Greek verb for reading, anaginōskō, is built on the verb for knowing, ginōskō, so the question rings: "Do you know what you know-again?" The little words ara ge add a note of doubt, "really." The eunuch's answer (8:31) is not embarrassment but humility, and it sets up a theme Luke loves: Scripture needs an interpreter who knows how it points to Jesus, as Jesus himself opened the Scriptures on the Emmaus road (Luke 24:27, 32, 45).
orig: Ἆρά γε γινώσκεις ἃ ἀναγινώσκεις; (ara ge ginōskeis ha anaginōskeis)

p: The verb is the one Jesus uses of the Spirit who will "lead" the disciples into all truth (John 16:13).
b: Hodēgeō means to lead on the way, a fitting word on a road. Jesus said the Spirit "will lead you in all the truth" (John 16:13), and Psalm 25:5 in Greek asks God, "Lead me in your truth." Here the Spirit has sent Philip (8:29) to be that guide. The scene mirrors the Emmaus story in Luke 24:13–35: a journey, a stranger who explains the Scriptures about the suffering Messiah, a sacrament (bread there, baptism here), and a sudden disappearance (Luke 24:31; Acts 8:39).

a: Like a sheep he was taken off to slaughter
p: The quotation follows the Greek of Isaiah 53:7–8 and stops just before the lines about sin.
b: Luke quotes the Septuagint almost word for word. The site's Plain of the Hebrew reads "Like a lamb that is taken off to slaughter, / like a ewe that falls silent in front of her shearers, / he did not open his mouth" (Isaiah 53:7), and in 53:8 "He was cut off from the land of the living" (Isaiah 53:8). The Greek of 53:8 is quite different (see 8:33). The quotation ends just before "because my people rebelled, the blow fell on him." Some (such as Cadbury and Conzelmann) take this as a sign that Luke stresses Jesus' innocent suffering and vindication more than an atoning death; others reply that a quotation calls to mind its whole passage and that Philip begins "from" this text (8:35).

a: Who will tell of his generation?
p: Genea can mean descendants, contemporaries or origin. Each gives a different sense.
b: The Greek follows the Septuagint of Isaiah 53:8, itself a hard rendering of difficult Hebrew. Descendants: who can speak of his offspring, since he died childless? A poignant line for a eunuch to read. Contemporaries: who will tell about the wicked generation that killed him? Origin: church fathers such as Irenaeus took it to mean that no one can describe his birth, either from the Father or from the virgin. The line before, "justice was snatched from him," can also be read as "his condemnation was taken away," that is, God reversed the verdict, a reading some find fits Luke's stress on vindication.
orig: τὴν γενεὰν αὐτοῦ τίς διηγήσεται; (tēn genean autou tis diēgēsetai)

a: whom does the prophet mean here?
p: The eunuch asks the question Jewish and Christian readers still debate about Isaiah 53.
b: The prophet himself or another prophet such as Jeremiah, who was "like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter" (Jeremiah 11:19). Israel, the servant named in Isaiah 41:8 and 49:3, suffering among the nations: the reading of Rashi and most medieval Jewish commentators. The Messiah: the Aramaic Targum of Isaiah applies 52:13 to the Messiah but turns the suffering onto his enemies; some later rabbinic texts link the Messiah with suffering. Christians, from the New Testament on, read the passage of Jesus. Philip's answer is not argued here but announced: he "told him the good news about Jesus" (8:35).

t: The silent one and the opened mouth
p: The passage said the servant "does not open his mouth." Luke answers with a mouth that opens to speak of him.
b: "Opened his mouth" is a biblical way of introducing solemn speech (Matthew 5:2; Acts 10:34), but here it stands right after Isaiah's "he does not open his mouth" (8:32). Luke may mean the echo: the servant who kept silent before his accusers now has witnesses who speak for him. Philip "started from this same passage," so Isaiah 53 is the doorway, not the whole message; the early church used it as a key text for Jesus' passion (Luke 22:37; 1 Peter 2:22–25).

a: What is stopping me from being baptized?
p: The verb kōlyō, "prevent," recurs at baptisms in Luke-Acts. Some scholars think it echoes an early baptismal question.
b: Jesus said of the children, "do not stop them" (Luke 18:16, mē kōlyete); Peter asks whether anyone can "stop" the baptism of Cornelius' household (10:47) and later asks who he was to stop God (11:17). Oscar Cullmann argued that "What prevents?" was a question asked in early baptismal services, to make sure nothing barred the candidate. Whether or not that is so, the question has special weight on this man's lips: a foreigner and a eunuch, whom the Law barred from the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:1), asks what now bars him, and the answer is nothing.
orig: τί κωλύει με βαπτισθῆναι; (ti kōlyei me baptisthēnai)

p: The KJV's 8:37 ("I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God") is a very old addition, known by AD 180.
b: The added verse gives the eunuch a confession before his baptism: Philip says, "If you believe with your whole heart, you may," and he answers, "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God." It is not in any early Greek manuscript, nor in the Byzantine majority, but Irenaeus quotes it about AD 180 (Against Heresies 3.12.8), so it is among the earliest additions to Acts. It probably records the question and answer used at baptisms in the second-century church. Some Baptist writers have used it to show that a confession of faith must come before baptism; most now argue the same point from 8:12 and 2:41 instead. Tap the bracketed line to read the verse.
orig: εἶπε δὲ ὁ Φίλιππος· εἰ πιστεύεις ἐξ ὅλης τῆς καρδίας, ἔξεστιν (Textus Receptus)

p: Baptists read this as immersion. Others say the words do not settle the method.
b: Luke says both Philip and the eunuch went "down into" (eis) the water and "came up from" it (8:39). Immersion: the most natural picture is of the baptized person being dipped, and "baptize" means "dip" (Baptist and Orthodox readings). Not decisive: since both men went into the water, the words describe the walk into the stream, not what happened there; the Didache, about AD 100, prefers running water but allows pouring water three times on the head when there is not enough (Didache 7). See the card on this chapter.

p: Like Elijah, Philip is carried off by the Spirit. The verb is the one Paul uses for being "caught up."
b: Obadiah feared that "the LORD's Spirit will carry you off to who knows where" (1 Kings 18:12), and the prophets' disciples said of Elijah, "The LORD's Spirit may have carried him off" (2 Kings 2:16). Ezekiel too was lifted and moved by the Spirit (Ezekiel 3:12–14; 8:3). The Greek verb harpazō, "snatch," is used of Paul "caught up" to the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:2–4) and of believers "caught up" to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). Some take Philip's removal as a miraculous transport; others as a sudden prompting that sent him off at once. Luke's words point to the first.
r: 1 Kings 18:12; 2 Kings 2:16; Ezekiel 3:12–14; Ezekiel 8:3; 2 Corinthians 12:2–4; 1 Thessalonians 4:17; Luke 24:31

a: he went on his way rejoicing
p: Irenaeus and Eusebius say he went home to preach. Ethiopian Christians honor him.
b: Irenaeus says the eunuch "was sent into the regions of Ethiopia to preach" (Against Heresies 3.12.8; compare 4.23.2, where he goes to be the herald of Christ in Ethiopia), and Eusebius calls him the first Gentile to receive the faith, who went home to proclaim it (Church History 2.1.13). Christianity became the faith of the court of Aksum, in what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea, about AD 340, through Frumentius, a story told by Rufinus. Aksum was not the same kingdom as Meroë, but Ethiopian Christians have long counted the eunuch as the start of their church. Joy (chara) marks salvation in Luke-Acts, as in Samaria (8:8).

p: Philip works his way up the coast through old Philistine country to Caesarea, where he will still be living in 21:8.
b: Azotus is the Greek name of Ashdod, one of the five Philistine cities (1 Samuel 5:1). From there the coastal road runs north through Jamnia, Joppa and Lydda's plain to Caesarea, Herod's great harbor city and the seat of the Roman governor. Peter will soon be found in the same towns (9:32–10:24), perhaps among believers Philip had reached. The Gospel is moving into mixed Jewish and Gentile country, preparing for the Gentile household at Caesarea in chapter 10.

a: Saul's every breath was still threat and murder
p: Threat and murder were the air Saul breathed. Paul later called himself a violent man.
b: Empneōn apeilēs kai phonou is literally "breathing in threat and murder." The verb means to breathe, so Saul lives and breathes his campaign. Paul's own words agree: "I persecuted the church of God beyond measure and tried to destroy it" (Galatians 1:13), and in 26:10–11 he admits voting for the death of believers and pursuing them to foreign cities. The Greek word for murder (phonos) makes clear that the persecution went beyond beatings.
orig: ἐμπνέων ἀπειλῆς καὶ φόνου (empneōn apeilēs kai phonou)

t: Did the high priest have power in Damascus?
p: He had no legal power in a foreign city, but great religious authority. Historians weigh the scene.
b: Damascus, about 135 miles (220 km) northeast of Jerusalem, had a large Jewish population (Josephus, Jewish War 2.561). The high priest, probably Caiaphas (until about AD 36), could not order arrests in a Roman or Nabatean-controlled city. But letters from him would carry weight with synagogue leaders, who could discipline their own members (compare the floggings Paul received, 2 Corinthians 11:24). Some point to 1 Maccabees 15:21, a Roman letter that asks foreign rulers to "hand them over to Simon the high priest, so that he may punish them according to their law" (1 Maccabees 15:21), as a precedent for extradition. Others (Haenchen, Pervo) think Luke has enlarged Saul's commission. Paul himself mentions only that he returned to Damascus (Galatians 1:17).

p: The first followers of Jesus called their movement "the Way," a path within Israel.
b: "The Way" (hē hodos) appears again in 18:25–26; 19:9, 23; 22:4; and 24:14, 22, where Paul says, "according to the Way, which they call a sect, I serve the God of our fathers." The name may come from Isaiah 40:3, "In the wilderness clear the way of the LORD!" (Isaiah 40:3), which John the Baptist's preaching made famous (Luke 3:4). The community at Qumran used the same verse of itself (Community Rule 1QS 8.13–16) and spoke of its members as those who walk perfectly in the way. The name shows how the movement first saw itself: not a new religion but the true path within Israel.

a: light from heaven flashed all around him
p: Paul says he "saw the Lord." Readers speak of a real appearance, a vision, or a natural crisis.
b: A bodily appearance of the risen Jesus: Paul lists it with the other resurrection appearances, "last of all ... he appeared also to me" (1 Corinthians 15:8), and Acts stresses light, a voice and blindness, outward signs others shared. A vision: Paul also speaks of God "revealing his Son in me" (Galatians 1:16), and 26:19 calls it a "heavenly vision"; many scholars, believers among them, think of a visionary experience that Paul took as a true meeting with the risen Lord (Segal compares Jewish visions of God's glory). A natural crisis: older rationalist readings proposed sunstroke, lightning, epilepsy or guilt over Stephen; these explain little of what followed. The three accounts (9; 22; 26) vary in details.

p: God calls a name twice at turning points. The voice uses the Hebrew form, Saoul.
b: "Abraham! Abraham!" (Genesis 22:11), "Jacob, Jacob" (Genesis 46:2), "Moses! Moses!" (Exodus 3:4), "Samuel! Samuel!" (1 Samuel 3:10): the doubled name marks a divine call. In narration Luke uses the Greek form Saulos, but the voice uses Saoul, the Hebrew name of Israel's first king from the same tribe of Benjamin (Philippians 3:5). In 26:14 Paul says the voice spoke "in the Hebrew language," probably meaning Aramaic. Ananias uses the same form (9:17).

p: Saul was hunting disciples, but the voice says "me." To harm Jesus' followers is to harm Jesus.
b: Jesus had said, "Whoever takes you in takes me in" (Matthew 10:40) and "every time you did it for one of these brothers of mine, even the least of them, you did it for me" (Matthew 25:40). The risen Lord now speaks the other side of that truth. Paul later developed the idea of the church as Christ's body (1 Corinthians 12:12–27), and Augustine often used this verse to teach that Christ the head speaks for his body on earth. The wording of 9:4–5 is kept the same as in 22:7–8 and 26:14–15, where the Greek is the same.

p: Kyrie can be a polite "sir" or a title for God. A voice from heaven calls for "Lord."
b: When a stranger is addressed, kyrie often means "sir" (John 4:11). Here Saul has been thrown down by light from heaven, a sign of God's presence, so most translations write "Lord": he knows he is facing something divine without yet knowing its name. The answer turns everything over: the heavenly Lord is Jesus, the crucified man whose followers Saul has been arresting. The same kyrie comes from Ananias (9:10, 13) and Cornelius (10:4) in their visions.

a: They heard the voice, but they saw no one.
t: Did the companions hear the voice?
p: Here the men hear the voice; in 22:9 they do not. Readers reconcile the two in several ways.
b: In 22:9 Paul says, "The men with me did see the light, but the voice of the one who spoke to me they did not hear." A grammar answer: here "hear" takes the genitive case, there the accusative, and some argued that the first means hearing a sound, the second understanding words; the rule does not hold everywhere in Greek, though the sense "hear without understanding" fits 22:9 well. A meaning answer: phōnē means both "voice" and "sound," so the men heard a noise but not words. Free retelling: Luke varies details in his three accounts and did not mind small tensions. All three accounts agree that the companions shared some outward sign, but only Saul met Jesus.
orig: ἀκούοντες μὲν τῆς φωνῆς (akouontes men tēs phōnēs)

p: Blind, fasting and praying (9:11), Saul spends three days in a kind of death before rising to new life.
b: Three days recalls Jonah in the fish and Jesus in the tomb, "on the third day" (Luke 24:7), a time of passing from death to life. Saul's blindness pictures the darkness he had lived in (26:18 speaks of turning people "from darkness to light"). His fasting before baptism matches early Christian practice: the Didache asks the one to be baptized to fast one or two days beforehand (Didache 7:4). Luke does not spell out a symbol, but the shape of the story invites one.

p: Not the Ananias of 5:1 or 23:2. Paul's retelling calls him devout and respected by Jews.
b: Ananias is the Greek form of Hananiah, "the LORD has been gracious," a common name. Here he is a disciple of Jesus in Damascus; in 22:12 Paul, speaking to a Jewish crowd, adds that he was "a devout man according to the Law, well spoken of by all the Jews living there." That shows how Jewish the Damascus believers still were. Nothing more is known of him; later tradition made him bishop of Damascus and a martyr. A chapel in Damascus is shown as his house.

p: Ananias answers as Abraham, Samuel and Isaiah did: "Here I am," the ready reply of a servant to God's call.
b: The Hebrew hinneni, "here I am," is the answer of those God calls: Abraham (Genesis 22:1), Moses (Exodus 3:4), Samuel (1 Samuel 3:4) and Isaiah ("Here I am! Send me," Isaiah 6:8). Luke tells Ananias' call in the language of the prophets. The double vision that follows, Saul seeing Ananias and Ananias told about Saul, is repeated in chapter 10 with Cornelius and Peter: God works on both sides.

p: Damascus still has its Straight Street, the long Roman main street running east to west through the old city.
b: Like many Greek and Roman cities, Damascus had a long colonnaded avenue crossing it from gate to gate, the Via Recta. Its line survives today as Straight Street (in Arabic, Midhat Pasha Souq and the street running to Bab Sharqi, the East Gate). The detail is the kind of local knowledge that historians such as Colin Hemer counted in favor of Luke's accuracy; critics reply that a famous street was easy to know about.

p: Tarsus was a rich Greek city in Cilicia, known for its schools. Paul was proud of it (21:39).
b: Tarsus, in southeast Asia Minor (modern Turkey), was the capital of the province of Cilicia, a trading city on the river Cydnus. Strabo praises its schools of philosophy. Paul was born there (22:3), held its citizenship (21:39) and Roman citizenship too (22:28), but was brought up in Jerusalem and trained under Gamaliel (22:3). He knew Greek well and called himself "a Hebrew born of Hebrews" and a Pharisee (Philippians 3:5). This mix of Greek city, Roman status and strict Jewish training fitted him for the mission of 9:15.

p: The first time Acts calls believers "saints," God's holy people. Ananias calls them Jesus' own saints.
b: Hoi hagioi, "the holy ones," was an Old Testament name for Israel as a people set apart (Exodus 19:6; Daniel 7:18, 22). Here it is used of believers in Jesus, and "your saints" makes them belong to Jesus, as Israel belonged to God. Paul uses the word for all believers ("to all the saints in Christ Jesus," Philippians 1:1); it does not yet mean outstanding Christians honored after death, the sense it later took in the church's calendar.

p: In the Old Testament people "call on the name of the LORD." Here believers call on the name of Jesus.
b: Peter quoted Joel at Pentecost: everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (2:21; Joel 2:32). From the start, believers did what Israel did toward God: they prayed to Jesus and called on his name (7:59; 22:16; 1 Corinthians 1:2, "all who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place"). Ananias' words show that early Jewish believers already gave Jesus the worship due to Israel's God, a point historians such as Larry Hurtado stressed.

p: "Vessel of choice" means a chosen tool or jar, picked to carry Jesus' name.
b: Skeuos eklogēs is literally "a vessel of choosing." A vessel is a container or tool; Jeremiah's potter shapes the clay as he pleases (Jeremiah 18:1–6), and Paul later writes of "vessels" of mercy (Romans 9:21–23) and of treasure in "clay jars" (2 Corinthians 4:7). The vessel "carries" the name. The three audiences, Gentiles, kings and Israelites, map Paul's career in Acts: Gentile cities, the rulers Sergius Paulus, Felix, Festus and Agrippa, and the synagogues and Jerusalem crowd. Paul saw himself as set apart from birth, like Jeremiah (Galatians 1:15; Jeremiah 1:5).

a: how many things he must suffer
p: The same "must" of God's plan that governed Jesus' suffering (Luke 24:26) now governs Paul's.
b: Luke uses dei, "it must be," for what God has planned: "The Messiah had to suffer all this and so go into his glory, didn't he?" (Luke 24:26). The persecutor will become the persecuted. Paul's list in 2 Corinthians 11:23–29 (beatings, stonings, shipwrecks, prison) shows how this came true, and Acts traces it from Damascus (9:23) to Rome. The Lord tells Ananias, not Saul, about the suffering, perhaps to reassure Ananias that this man's commission will cost him dearly.

p: Ananias greets his former enemy as "brother": a fellow believer, or a fellow Jew.
b: Jews called one another brothers (2:29; 22:1), and believers in Jesus used the word for each other (9:30). Ananias, who had just protested about Saul's violence (9:13–14), uses it before Saul is baptized. Many readers see in this greeting the first sign of the reconciliation Saul will later preach. Ananias uses the Hebrew form of the name, Saoul, as the voice did on the road (9:4).

a: you will be filled with the Holy Spirit
t: The Spirit and baptism in Saul's case
p: Saul is to be filled with the Spirit through Ananias' hands, and then baptized. Acts follows no single order.
b: In Acts the Spirit comes in different orders: with repentance and baptism (2:38), after baptism through the apostles' hands (8:16–17), before baptism while Peter is still speaking (10:44–48), and right after baptism with the laying on of hands (19:5–6). Here Ananias, not an apostle, lays hands on Saul, and Luke does not say exactly when the Spirit came. Many conclude that Luke records what happened rather than laying down a rule; others build a pattern from the cases, either of one event (conversion-initiation, Dunn) or of a later empowering (Pentecostal teaching). Saul is "filled" as the apostles were (2:4; 4:31), for bold witness (9:20).

p: Luke says "something like scales" fell away. English took the phrase into ordinary speech for a sudden insight.
b: Lepides are flakes or scales, like a fish's. Luke says only "as if," describing how it seemed. A similar picture is in Tobit, where Tobit "flaked the white films off from the corners of his eyes" (Tobit 11:13) after the fish gall was applied. The nineteenth-century writer W. K. Hobart argued that such words showed Luke was a physician; H. J. Cadbury answered that educated non-doctors used the same vocabulary. The phrase "the scales fell from his eyes" became an English idiom from this verse.

p: The only place in Acts where Jesus is called "the Son of God." It matches Galatians 1:16.
b: Paul wrote that God "was pleased to reveal his Son in me, so that I might preach him among the Gentiles" (Galatians 1:16), and he opens Romans with Jesus "declared to be the Son of God in power ... by his resurrection" (Romans 1:4). In Acts the title appears only here, though Paul quotes Psalm 2:7 in 13:33. To Jewish hearers in a synagogue the title first meant God's chosen king, as in Psalm 2, with the deeper sense the church came to confess.

p: The verb portheō, "destroy, ravage," appears only here and in Paul's own account in Galatians 1:13, 23.
b: Paul uses this verb of himself twice in Galatians: he says he was trying to destroy the church of God (Galatians 1:13), and that the churches of Judea heard that their old persecutor now preached the faith he had once tried to destroy (Galatians 1:23). There Paul uses the imperfect tense, "kept trying to destroy." Here Luke uses a simple past, "the one who ravaged," so the Plain does not add "tried." Luke puts the same rare verb in the mouths of the Damascus Jews. Whether Luke knew Galatians (most scholars doubt it) or both reflect how people talked about Saul, the match shows that this was how Paul's turnabout was remembered. The verb was used of sacking a city.

p: The verb means to bring things together. Saul argued by setting Scriptures side by side with what had happened to Jesus.
b: Symbibazō means to join or put together, and so to prove by combining evidence. Luke shows Paul doing this again in the synagogue at Thessalonica, explaining that the Messiah had to suffer and rise (17:2–3). The Damascus Jews are "confused" (synchynnō, the word for the crowd's bewilderment at Pentecost, 2:6). "This man is the Messiah" is the core claim Paul will make throughout Acts (17:3; 18:5).

p: Paul says he went to Arabia and waited three years before Jerusalem (Galatians 1:17–18).
b: In Galatians Paul insists that after his call he did not go up to Jerusalem but "went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus. Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem" (Galatians 1:17–18). Arabia here means the Nabatean kingdom east and south of Damascus. Most fit the Arabia stay into Luke's "considerable time" (literally "enough days"), between 9:22 and 9:23. Some place it before 9:20. Critical scholars note that Acts compresses Paul's early years and has him go to Jerusalem sooner than Galatians suggests, so they prefer Paul's account where the two differ. On Paul's dates see the topic paul.

p: Luke blames "the Jews" for the plot. Paul's own account names the governor of King Aretas.
b: In 2 Corinthians 11:32–33 Paul writes that in Damascus "the ethnarch of King Aretas was guarding the city" to seize him, and that he was let down in a basket through a window in the wall. Aretas IV ruled the Nabateans (about 9 BC to AD 40). Some harmonize: Jewish leaders and the Nabatean official worked together, Paul having angered both, perhaps by preaching in Arabia. Others see Luke's habit of naming "the Jews" as Paul's opponents (13:45; 14:19; 17:5), which later readers turned against all Jews. Here the phrase means the leaders of the Jewish community in Damascus, not the Jewish people as a whole; many Jews in Acts believe (see the topic anti-judaism).

t: Down the wall in a basket
p: Paul tells this escape in 2 Corinthians 11:33. Rahab and Michal had let men down too.
b: Paul uses the story to boast of his weakness: "I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall, and escaped his hands" (2 Corinthians 11:33). Luke's word for the basket, spyris, is the big hamper of the feeding of the four thousand (Mark 8:8); Paul uses sarganē, a rope basket. Old Testament echoes are close: Rahab "let them down by a rope through the window" (Joshua 2:15), and "Michal lowered David through the window" (1 Samuel 19:12). The persecutor now flees like a hunted man.

t: Saul's first visit in Acts and in Galatians
p: Acts has Saul meet "the apostles"; Galatians says he saw only Peter and James.
b: Paul swears in Galatians that on this visit he stayed fifteen days with Cephas (Peter), saw no other apostle except James the Lord's brother, and remained "unknown by face to the churches of Judea" (Galatians 1:18–22). Harmonizers note that Peter and James could be called "the apostles" in a summary, and that Paul's oath is aimed at denying that he got his gospel from Jerusalem, not at describing every meeting. Critical scholars (Haenchen, Knox, Pervo) think Luke tied Paul more closely to the Jerusalem leaders than he was, in keeping with Luke's picture of one united church. Readers who want Paul's own account should start from Galatians.

p: Joseph Barnabas, the Levite from Cyprus (4:36), takes the risk of trusting Saul. He will later bring him to Antioch.
b: Barnabas was introduced as the generous Levite from Cyprus whom the apostles named son of encouragement (4:36–37). Here he lives up to it, "taking hold" of Saul and speaking for him. Luke does not say how Barnabas knew Saul's story; some suggest they had met before, since both were Greek-speaking Jews of the diaspora. Barnabas later fetches Saul from Tarsus to Antioch (11:25–26) and leads the first mission with him (13–14), until they part over Mark (15:36–41).

p: Greek-speaking Jews: the group that had opposed Stephen (6:9), and Saul had stood with them.
b: Hellēnistai were Jews whose main language was Greek (6:1). The synagogues of Freedmen, Cyrenians, Alexandrians, Cilicians and Asians had argued with Stephen and brought him to trial (6:9). Saul, from Cilicia, may once have been one of them. Now he takes Stephen's place in the argument and meets Stephen's danger: they "set about trying to kill him." The "Grecians" of the KJV are not Greeks but Greek-speaking Jews.

a: sent him on his way to Tarsus
p: Saul vanishes from Acts for years, until Barnabas finds him (11:25). Paul says Syria and Cilicia.
b: Paul writes that after his first Jerusalem visit he "went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia" (Galatians 1:21), and fourteen years later went up again (Galatians 2:1). Acts is silent about these years, perhaps a decade. Many scholars think Paul was already preaching to Gentiles there; some of the hardships of 2 Corinthians 11:23–27 may belong to this time. In 22:17–21 Paul tells of a vision in the temple in which the Lord sent him away from Jerusalem "to the Gentiles."

a: Across all Judea, Galilee and Samaria
t: A summary: the church at peace
p: One of Luke's growth summaries, and the only mention of a church in Galilee in Acts.
b: Luke punctuates Acts with summaries that say the word or the church grew, and each closes a section. This one closes the Samaria and Saul stories before Peter's journey to the coast. The persecutor is converted, so the church has peace. "Judea, Galilee and Samaria" covers the old land of Israel: the plan of 1:8 has reached its second stage. "Built up" is building language (compare Matthew 16:18), and "encouragement" (paraklēsis) is related to Jesus' name for the Spirit in John, the Advocate (paraklētos). Galilee, where Jesus' ministry began, appears nowhere else in Acts as a place with a church.

p: Lydda, on the road from Jerusalem to Joppa, already had believers when Peter came.
b: Lydda, the Old Testament Lod (1 Chronicles 8:12), lay about 11 miles (18 km) southeast of Joppa, at the edge of the coastal plain of Sharon, famous for its flowers (Song of Songs 2:1; Isaiah 35:2). It is today the city of Lod near Israel's main airport. Luke does not say who founded the church there: perhaps Philip (8:40) or believers scattered from Jerusalem (8:4). Peter's tour mirrors his visit to Samaria (8:14) and moves him toward Joppa and Caesarea.

t: Eight years, or since he was eight?
p: The Greek ex etōn oktō can mean he had been bedridden for eight years, or since the age of eight.
b: The Greek can mean either. Ex with a span of time can count the years up to now, as in 24:10 (ek pollōn etōn, of Felix's many years as judge); Luke 8:43 says the same sort of thing with apo, of the woman ill for twelve years. Most translations take it as the length of the illness, as the Plain does; a minority read it as "since he was eight years old." Either way the healing reverses a long, hopeless condition. Luke does not say whether Aeneas was already a believer; he has a Greek name, from the Trojan hero of Homer and Virgil.

p: Peter's words point away from himself, and the scene recalls Jesus healing a paralyzed man (Luke 5:17–26).
b: Peter says, "Jesus Christ is healing you," as at the temple gate he had healed in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth (3:6, 16). Jesus told the paralyzed man in Capernaum, "get up, pick up your cot, and go to your house" (Luke 5:24). "Make your own bed" (strōson seautō) can mean either spread your bedding or set your table (prepare a couch for a meal, as in Mark 14:15). The man who was carried can now look after himself. The healing at Lydda and the raising at Joppa repeat, on a smaller scale, the two healings of Jairus' story and the paralyzed man in the Gospel.

p: Mathētria, "woman disciple," is used only here in the New Testament. Luke counts women as disciples in their own right.
b: The feminine form mathētria is rare in Greek and unique in the New Testament. Luke often shows women among Jesus' followers (Luke 8:1–3; 10:38–42; 24:1–10) and in the church (1:14; 12:12; 16:14–15; 18:26). Tabitha's "good works" and alms were the kind of acts of mercy Jewish piety prized (compare Tobit 12:9), and she is the only woman in the New Testament called a disciple by name.

p: Tabitha is Aramaic for "gazelle"; Dorcas is the Greek word for the same animal.
b: The gazelle was a picture of grace and beauty (Song of Songs 2:9; Proverbs 6:5). Bilingual names were common in a port like Joppa, where Aramaic and Greek were both spoken. Readers of Mark notice that Peter's words in 9:40, "Tabitha, get up," sound almost like Jesus' Aramaic words to Jairus' daughter, Talitha koum, "little girl, get up" (Mark 5:41): one letter apart in Aramaic. Peter, who was in the room that day, repeats what he saw Jesus do.

p: Jewish custom washed the dead before burial. Laying her in an upper room instead of burying her at once may show hope.
b: Washing the body was a regular act of love; the Mishnah allows it even on the Sabbath (Mishnah Shabbat 23:5). In Judea the dead were usually buried the same day. The disciples instead laid Tabitha in an upstairs room and sent for Peter, who was about three hours' walk away. Luke does not say they expected a miracle, but the stories of Elijah and Elisha, who raised children in upper rooms (1 Kings 17:19; 2 Kings 4:10, 21), were well known.

p: Widows were among the poorest people of the ancient world. Tabitha clothed them.
b: A widow without sons often had no income. The Law commanded care for her (Deuteronomy 24:17–21), and the Jerusalem church had a daily distribution to widows (6:1). Later letters speak of an enrolled group of widows who prayed and served (1 Timothy 5:3–16). The widows show Peter the chitōnes, tunics worn next to the skin, and himatia, outer cloaks, that Dorcas "used to make": she was their patron. Their tears are both grief and a plea.

p: Peter sends everyone out, kneels, prays and speaks to the dead woman, as Elisha and Jesus had done.
b: Elisha "went in and closed the door, with only the two of them inside, and he prayed to the LORD" (2 Kings 4:33). Jesus put the mourners out and took the girl by the hand, saying "Talitha koum" (Mark 5:40–41; Luke 8:51–55). Peter prays first, because the power is not his own, then commands. Luke lines up Peter's deeds with Jesus' and later Paul's (raising Eutychus, 20:9–12), to show the same Lord at work through each.

p: Tanners handled carcasses and were often unclean. Peter's lodging hints at loosening lines.
b: Tanning used dead animals' skins, lime, urine and dung, so tanneries were smelly and kept outside towns; the Mishnah says a tannery must be at least fifty cubits from a town (Mishnah Bava Batra 2:9) and lets a wife seek divorce from a husband who becomes a tanner (Mishnah Ketubot 7:10). Touching carcasses made a person unclean until evening (Leviticus 11:39–40). Many see Peter's stay as a first step toward the house of Cornelius. Others note that tanning was a lawful trade and that Luke may mention it only to locate the house "by the sea" (10:6), where water for tanning was at hand.

t: A centurion of the Italian Cohort
p: A centurion led about a hundred men. An "Italian" cohort is attested in Syria.
b: Caesarea, Herod's harbor city, was the Roman governor's headquarters and a largely Gentile town. A cohort (speira) was a unit of about 500 to 1,000 soldiers; the auxiliary troops stationed in Judea were mostly raised locally, from Caesarea and Sebaste. An inscription records a "Second Italian Cohort of Roman citizens" in Syria by AD 69. Some object that from AD 41 to 44 Judea was ruled by King Agrippa I, not by Rome, so Roman units may not have been at Caesarea then; others date the Cornelius story before 41, or think a retired or detached officer lived there. Luke's centurions are friendly figures: the one at Capernaum loved the Jewish nation (Luke 7:1–10), the one at the cross praised God (Luke 23:47), and Julius treated Paul kindly (27:3).

a: he and his whole household feared God
p: Cornelius worshiped Israel's God, prayed and gave alms, but was not circumcised: a God-fearer.
b: Luke uses "those who fear God" and "worshipers of God" for Gentiles attached to the synagogue (13:16, 26; 16:14; 17:4). Josephus mentions "those who revered God" sending gifts to the temple (Jewish Antiquities 14.110), and an inscription from Aphrodisias in Asia Minor, published in 1987, lists Jews, converts and a separate group of theosebeis, "God-worshipers," who supported the synagogue. A. T. Kraabel once argued that Luke invented the class; the Aphrodisias find persuaded most scholars that God-fearers were real, though the term was not fixed. In Jewish eyes such people were righteous Gentiles; in the church's eyes, here, the ground prepared for the gospel.

a: much in alms to the people
p: Eleēmosynē, "mercy given," was one of the pillars of Jewish piety with prayer and fasting. "The people" means Israel.
b: Jesus named almsgiving, prayer and fasting together (Matthew 6:1–18), and the book of Tobit says, "Alms rescue from death, and they cleanse away every sin" (Tobit 12:9). In Luke-Acts "the people" (ho laos) almost always means Israel, so Cornelius' charity went to poor Jews. Luke shows a Gentile living out Jewish piety before he hears the gospel. Readers have long asked whether such good works earn God's favor; Luke's answer comes in 10:4 and 10:35, and in 11:14, where the angel promises words by which Cornelius will be saved.

p: The ninth hour, about 3 p.m., was the time of the afternoon offering at the temple and a set time of prayer (3:1).
b: Peter and John went up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour (3:1), when the afternoon lamb was offered. Cornelius keeps the same hour in Caesarea. Daniel's angel Gabriel came to him "at the time of the evening offering" (Daniel 9:21), and Psalm 141 links prayer and that offering: "my hands raised high as the evening grain offering" (Psalm 141:2). The Plain keeps "ninth hour" because Luke's readers would hear its link to the temple; days were counted from sunrise.

p: Mnēmosynon is the Greek word for the "token portion" of an offering. Prayer counts as one.
b: In Leviticus the priest burns a handful of the grain offering as its "token portion" (Leviticus 2:2); the Greek translation calls this a mnēmosynon, a reminder, because it reminds God of the worshiper. The angel says Cornelius' prayers and alms "have gone up" like the smoke of that offering. Tobit's angel says, "I was the one who carried the memorial of your prayer before the Lord's glory" (Tobit 12:12). A Gentile, who could not offer at the altar in Jerusalem, has his worship accepted all the same.
r: Leviticus 2:2; Leviticus 2:9; Psalm 141:2; Tobit 12:12; Hebrews 13:16; Philippians 4:18; Revelation 8:3–4

a: Peter climbed up to the flat roof to pray
t: Prayer on the roof at noon
p: Flat roofs were used for rest and prayer. Devout Jews prayed at midday too.
b: Houses in the land had flat roofs reached by an outside stair, used for drying, sleeping and quiet. The sixth hour was noon. A psalm speaks of praying "At evening, at morning, at midday" (Psalm 55:17), and Daniel prayed three times a day (Daniel 6:10). On the coast at Joppa, Peter could see the Mediterranean, the sea that led to the Gentile world; it was from Joppa that Jonah once fled from God's call to a Gentile city (Jonah 1:3).

p: Ekstasis means being "outside oneself": a waking vision. Peter's hunger gives the vision its subject, food.
b: The word gives English "ecstasy," but here it means a state in which the senses are taken over by a vision (compare 22:17, Paul in the temple). Luke notes that Peter was hungry and a meal was being made below; the vision speaks to him in the language of his body. Many readers see God using the ordinary, not overriding it. The same Greek word describes the people's astonishment at healings (3:10).

p: An opened heaven marks a revelation: Ezekiel's visions, Jesus' baptism, Stephen's death.
b: "The heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God" begins Ezekiel's book (Ezekiel 1:1). At Jesus' baptism "the heavens opened" (Matthew 3:16), and Stephen saw "the heavens opened" and the Son of Man standing (7:56). Here the opened heaven lets down not a throne but a sheet of animals: the revelation concerns everyday food and, through it, who may sit at the same table.
r: Ezekiel 1:1; Matthew 3:16; Luke 3:21; John 1:51; 7:56; Revelation 4:1; Revelation 19:11

p: The sheet holds every kind of animal, clean and unclean mixed, in the three groups of Genesis and the Law.
b: Four-footed animals, creeping things and birds are the classes of creation (Genesis 1:24; 6:20) and of the food laws (Leviticus 11). Noah took every kind into the ark, and God told him, "two of each will come to you to be kept alive" (Genesis 6:20). Peter sees them together, and many think that by Jewish rules a clean animal touching an unclean one would make the whole lot "common." That is why he refuses even though some clean animals must be there. Creeping things were among the most strongly forbidden (Leviticus 11:41–44).
r: Genesis 1:24; Genesis 6:20; Genesis 9:3; Leviticus 11:1–47; Leviticus 11:41–44; Romans 1:23

p: Thyō often means to sacrifice, but also simply to slaughter for food, as with the fattened calf (Luke 15:23).
b: The verb thyō is used of sacrifice in the temple and in pagan worship (14:13, 18), but also of ordinary slaughter for a meal (Luke 15:23, 27, 30). Deuteronomy allowed meat to be killed and eaten anywhere, away from the altar (Deuteronomy 12:15). The command here is the plain one: kill for food and eat. The words "Get up, Peter; kill and eat" are kept the same in 11:7, where Peter tells the story.

p: Peter answers with the same Greek word Ezekiel used when told to eat unclean food: Mēdamōs, "Not at all!"
b: When God told Ezekiel to bake bread over dung, the prophet protested in the Greek text, "Mēdamōs, Lord God of Israel!": he had never eaten anything unclean (Ezekiel 4:14). Daniel resolved not to defile himself with the king's food (Daniel 1:8), and in the Maccabean persecution many Jews "accepted death rather than be made unclean by food and profane the holy covenant" (1 Maccabees 1:63). Peter's refusal stands in that faithful tradition; it is not stubbornness. That makes the voice's answer all the more surprising.

p: Two different words: "unclean" for what the Law forbids, and "common" for what is ordinary or made impure by contact.
b: Akathartos, "unclean," is the Law's word for forbidden animals (Leviticus 11:4). Koinos, "common," meant ordinary, not holy, and in Jewish Greek came to mean defiled, as in 1 Maccabees and Mark 7:2 ("with common hands"). A clean animal could become "common" by contact with unclean things. Peter has kept both rules. The voice answers only about "common" (10:15), and Peter later applies both words to people (10:28). The Plain keeps both English words, as this site does in Peter's retelling in 11:8–9.

a: What God has made clean, you must not call common.
t: Did the vision end the food laws?
p: Peter applies the vision to people (10:28). Whether it also abolished the food laws for Jewish believers is debated.
b: Food and people: most Christian readers take the vision as declaring all foods clean, as Mark 7:19 notes of Jesus' teaching and Paul says in Romans 14:14 and 1 Timothy 4:4, and as a picture of welcoming Gentiles. People only: Peter himself draws only one lesson, that "no human being is to be called common or unclean" (10:28), and in 11:3 the complaint is about eating with Gentiles, not eating pork; some Messianic Jewish and Seventh-day Adventist teachers hold that the food laws still stand. Table fellowship: many scholars think the real issue was sharing meals, since Jewish believers would eat Gentile food at Gentile tables; compare Peter at Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14). See the card at Matthew 15:11.

p: Three times makes it certain. Peter had denied Jesus three times and been asked three times.
b: Repeating a revelation confirms it (Genesis 41:32, where Pharaoh's dream comes twice "because the matter is fixed by God"). Peter's life has threes: three denials (Luke 22:61) and three questions by the lake (John 21:15–17). Luke does not draw the link, but the old disciple who needed to hear things three times hears this one three times, and still is "at a loss" (10:17).

p: God prepares both sides: an angel for Cornelius, a sheet for Peter, and perfect timing.
b: Luke used the same pattern with Saul and Ananias (9:10–12). Ancient Greek and Roman writers also told of "double dreams," two people given matching visions so that they would meet, and scholars have studied the parallels. The verdict: Luke shares a storytelling form known in his world, which made divine guidance clear to readers, but the content is his own, and the Old Testament has its own paired revelations (Genesis 41; Daniel 2). The timing ("Just then") is the point: God's word and God's events arrive together.

p: The verb diakrinomai means "doubt" but also "make a distinction." Luke plays on both: go, and do not discriminate.
b: In the middle voice diakrinomai means to waver or doubt (Matthew 21:21; Romans 4:20). In the active it means to distinguish or discriminate. When Peter retells the story, the Spirit told him to go making no distinction (11:12), and at the council he says God made no distinction between Jews and Gentiles (15:9). The words remember a single lesson: the barrier between Jew and Gentile is not God's last word.

a: the whole Jewish nation speaks well of him
p: Luke's other good centurion is a friend of the Jews too: "He loves our nation" (Luke 7:5).
b: In Luke 7:1–10 Jewish elders plead for a centurion at Capernaum, and Jesus praises his faith without entering his house. Here a centurion has God's attention, and Peter will enter his house. The messengers stress Cornelius' standing with Jews, perhaps so that Peter will not refuse. Their report adds a detail the reader knew from 10:4–6: the angel told Cornelius to "listen to the words you bring," which 11:14 spells out: words by which he and his household will be saved.

a: put them up as his guests
p: A Jew could host Gentiles more easily than eat in their homes, but Peter is crossing a line.
b: Xenizō means to receive as a guest, with food and lodging. Jewish practice was stricter about eating Gentile food and entering Gentile homes than about having Gentiles as guests. Still, sharing a roof and a meal with Cornelius' men starts what the next day completes. Six Jewish believers from Joppa come along (11:12), as witnesses: a wise step, since Peter will have to answer for what he does (11:2–3).

p: Proskyneō means both to bow low and to worship. Peter refuses it: no human being may take what belongs to God.
b: As in the Gospels, the verb covers a gesture of honor to a superior and the worship of God. A Roman officer bowing to a Jewish fisherman is startling either way. Peter lifts him up with "I myself am only a human being," as Paul and Barnabas refuse worship at Lystra (14:14–15) and the angel refuses John in Revelation (Revelation 19:10; 22:8–9). Herod Agrippa, by contrast, accepts the cry that he is a god and is struck down (12:22–23). Some readers set this beside later claims to Peter's honor in the church; Catholic writers reply that honor given to a person is different from worship.

a: keeping company with a foreigner or visiting one is not allowed
t: "Not allowed": a custom, not a law of Moses
p: No law of Moses forbids visiting a Gentile. Peter uses a word for what custom or decency forbids.
b: Athemitos means "against custom, taboo," not "against the Torah." Jews in Peter's day did trade and talk with Gentiles every day. The worry was eating their food, which might be unclean or offered to idols, and entering their homes, which some held to be unclean: the Mishnah says "the dwelling places of Gentiles are unclean" (Oholot 18:7). Jubilees urges, "Separate yourself from the nations, and do not eat with them" (Jubilees 22:16). Practice varied, as E. P. Sanders has shown, but the line was real enough that Peter's entering was news (11:3). "Foreigner" (allophylos) is the Greek Old Testament's word for Philistines and other outsiders.

p: Ancient counting included the first and last days. By our counting the vision was three days earlier.
b: Day one: Cornelius' vision and the messengers leave (10:3–8). Day two: they reach Joppa (10:9). Day three: Peter sets out (10:23). Day four: they arrive (10:24). The Greek "from the fourth day until this hour" counts all four, the way Jesus rose "on the third day" after a Friday death. Some modern Bibles write "three days ago" to match our way of counting; the Plain keeps "four" as the Greek has it.

p: Cornelius describes the angel as "a man" in bright clothing, as Luke describes the angels at the tomb and the ascension.
b: At the empty tomb "two men" stood by the women "in dazzling clothes" (Luke 24:4), and at the ascension two men in white (1:10). Luke's angels often look like men, and their clothes show where they come from. Cornelius calls him "a man," the narrator "an angel of God" (10:3): both are true.

p: The Greek word means "face-taker": one who judges by a person's face, rank or nation. It comes from a Hebrew idiom.
b: Prosōpolēmptēs is built from the Hebrew phrase "lift up the face," meaning to show favor or partiality. The Law says of God, "He does not play favorites, and he does not take a bribe" (Deuteronomy 10:17), and judges are told the same (2 Chronicles 19:7). Paul uses the idea for Jew and Gentile alike before God's judgment (Romans 2:11). Peter had known the verse all his life; what he now "grasps" is that it applies to who may belong to God's people.
orig: οὐκ ἔστιν προσωπολήμπτης ὁ θεός (ouk estin prosōpolēmptēs ho theos)
r: Deuteronomy 10:17; 2 Chronicles 19:7; Job 34:19; Romans 2:11; Galatians 2:6; James 2:1; 1 Peter 1:17

p: Does Peter mean that God-fearing Gentiles are saved without the gospel? Readers answer differently.
b: Dektos, "welcome, acceptable," is the word the Greek Isaiah uses for foreigners' offerings that "will be welcome on my altar" (Isaiah 56:7). Acceptable to receive the gospel: most readers note that Cornelius still needed words by which he would be saved (11:14) and forgiveness in Jesus' name (10:43); God accepts people of any nation who seek him and brings them to Christ. Accepted already: some, appealing also to Romans 2:14–16, have read the verse as support for the salvation of devout people outside the church; Catholic teaching since Vatican II speaks of those who seek God sincerely without knowing the gospel (Lumen Gentium 16). See the card on "no other name" at 4:12.

p: Peter joins Psalm 107:20 ("He sent his word") with Isaiah 52:7 ("who makes peace heard").
b: The Psalm says, "He sent his word to heal them" (Psalm 107:20), and Isaiah praises the feet of the one "who brings good news, / who makes peace heard" (Isaiah 52:7). Peace (eirēnē, Hebrew shalom) is more than an end to war: it is wholeness and right relations with God and others. In a Roman officer's house, where "peace" meant the pax Romana won by the emperor, the claim that peace comes "by way of Jesus Christ" is pointed. Paul echoes the same texts when he speaks of Christ making Jew and Gentile one (Ephesians 2:14–17).
r: Psalm 107:20; Isaiah 52:7; Nahum 1:15; Luke 2:14; Ephesians 2:14–17; Romans 10:15

t: "Lord of all" and a broken sentence
p: The Greek of 10:36–38 is famously tangled. Inside it stands a short cry: "he is Lord of all," Jew and Gentile alike.
b: The sentence begins "the word that he sent" with no main verb until "you know" in 10:37, and the grammar never quite resolves; some think the roughness shows an Aramaic source or a speech set down from memory, others simply Peter's excitement. The Plain splits it into sentences. "Lord of all" (pantōn kyrios) was a title for God in Jewish prayer and, in other forms, for gods and emperors. Peter says it of Jesus in a Gentile house, and Paul says the same: "the same Lord is Lord of all, rich to all who call on him" (Romans 10:12).
orig: οὗτός ἐστιν πάντων κύριος (houtos estin pantōn kyrios)

p: Peter's summary runs from John's baptism to the resurrection: the outline of Mark's Gospel.
b: C. H. Dodd argued that the speeches in Acts preserve the early church's preaching (the kerygma), and that this sermon follows the same outline as Mark: John's baptism, Jesus anointed, healing in Galilee, death in Jerusalem, resurrection, appearances, coming judgment. An early tradition from Papias says Mark wrote down Peter's preaching (Eusebius, Church History 3.39.15). Others see the speeches as Luke's own compositions, in the way ancient historians wrote speeches suited to the speaker (Thucydides 1.22), and the outline as Luke summarizing his own Gospel. Many take a middle view: Luke's wording, built on early tradition.

a: God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power
p: "Messiah" means anointed. Jesus was anointed with the Spirit, as Isaiah 61 promised.
b: Isaiah's servant says, "The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on me, / because the LORD has anointed me / to bring good news to the humble" (Isaiah 61:1), the text Jesus read at Nazareth (Luke 4:18). Luke places the anointing at Jesus' baptism, when the Spirit came down on him (Luke 3:21–22; compare the prayer in Acts 4:27). Kings and priests were anointed with oil (1 Samuel 16:13); Jesus' anointing is with the Spirit, and so the anointed one, the Messiah, is shown in deeds of healing.

p: Euergetōn means acting as a benefactor. Rulers in the Greek world took the title "Benefactor"; Jesus earned it.
b: Kings and wealthy patrons were honored as euergetai, "benefactors," on inscriptions across the eastern Mediterranean, and Jesus mentions the practice: "those who use their power over them are given the title 'Benefactor'" (Luke 22:25). A Roman officer would know the word well. Peter uses it of Jesus, whose benefactions were healing those "the devil was crushing under his power." The verb for that, katadynasteuō, means to oppress as a tyrant: Jesus' good works were a rescue from a hostile ruler.

p: In Jerusalem Peter told his hearers that they had killed him (2:23; 3:15). In a Gentile house he says "they."
b: "They" means the people of Jerusalem and their leaders, as 13:27 spells out, together with the Romans who carried out the crucifixion (4:27). Peter's Jerusalem speeches accuse their hearers directly and call them to repent. Here the hearers had no part in it. Readers who used Acts to blame all Jews for Jesus' death ignored this distinction, and the church's own teaching has rejected that blame (the Catholic Nostra Aetate 4, 1965, and many Protestant statements). See the topic anti-judaism.

p: "On a tree" recalls Deuteronomy 21:22–23, where the hanged man is cursed by God.
b: The Law says, "his body must not stay on the tree overnight ... for a man who is hanged is cursed by God" (Deuteronomy 21:23). By Jesus' time the verse was applied to crucifixion: the Temple Scroll from Qumran speaks of hanging a traitor on a tree so that he dies (11QTemple 64:6–13). Peter uses "tree" (xylon) of the cross here and in 5:30; Paul says Christ "became a curse for us" (Galatians 3:13), and 1 Peter 2:24 says he carried our sins "on the tree." What looked like proof that God had rejected Jesus became, after the resurrection, the place where he took the curse.

p: Peter's proof is ordinary: we ate and drank with him. The risen Jesus was no ghost.
b: In Luke 24 the risen Jesus breaks bread at Emmaus (Luke 24:30–31) and eats a piece of fish before the disciples, saying "A spirit has no flesh and bones, the way you see that I have" (Luke 24:39; compare Luke 24:40–43); Acts 1:4 may mean he was "eating with" them. The witnesses were "picked beforehand" (procheirotoneō, literally "chosen by show of hands in advance"), the same root as appointing elders in 14:23. Peter's point to Gentiles: the claim rests on people who knew him before and after.

a: judge the living and the dead
t: Judge of the living and the dead
p: The risen Jesus is appointed judge of all, a phrase the Apostles' Creed kept.
b: Paul tells the Athenians that God has set a day to judge the world by a man he has appointed (17:31). The same pairing "the living and the dead" appears in 2 Timothy 4:1 and 1 Peter 4:5, and the creeds of the church kept it. For a Gentile audience with no knowledge of the Jewish hope, Peter's message joins forgiveness (10:43) with a coming judgment, as Daniel's "one like a son of man" receives authority over all nations (Daniel 7:13–14).

a: Every prophet bears witness to him
p: Peter claims the whole prophetic witness, as Jesus had taught (Luke 24:27, 44–47).
b: Luke's Gospel ends with Jesus opening the disciples' minds to see that "repentance for the forgiveness of sins" must be preached in his name to all nations, as written in Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms (Luke 24:44–47). Texts the church read this way include Isaiah 53:5–6, 11 (the servant bearing sins), Jeremiah 31:34 ("I will forgive their guilt") and Joel 2:32 (whoever calls on the name). "All who believe" is the key for Gentile hearers: no other condition is named.

a: the Holy Spirit fell on everyone
p: Here the Spirit comes before baptism, while Peter is still preaching: a Gentile Pentecost.
b: Peter tells Jerusalem that the Spirit fell on them just as on the apostles at the beginning (11:15). God interrupts the sermon, so no one can say the apostles decided who belonged. For many the order shows that the Spirit is God's free gift, not bound to rites. For sacramental churches it is an exception that proves the rule, since Peter still has them baptized (10:47–48). For Pentecostals the tongues of 10:46 are the outward sign of this baptism in the Spirit. See the cards at 8:14–17 and 19:1–7.

p: Jewish believers. The phrase later names a party that insisted on circumcision.
b: Hoi ek peritomēs means "those from circumcision," that is, Jews. Here it simply describes Peter's six Jewish companions from Joppa (11:12). In 11:2 "those of the circumcision" criticize Peter, and in Galatians 2:12 Paul uses it of a party from James whose arrival made Peter stop eating with Gentiles. Their astonishment shows how unexpected this was even for believers: "even on the Gentiles." "Poured out" echoes Joel 2:28, quoted at Pentecost (2:17).
orig: οἱ ἐκ περιτομῆς πιστοί (hoi ek peritomēs pistoi)

p: The same sign as at Pentecost. Known languages or prayer-speech? Readers differ.
b: Lalein glōssais means "to speak in tongues" or "languages." At Pentecost the crowd heard their own languages (2:6–11); in 1 Corinthians 12–14 tongues need interpreting. Peter calls Caesarea the same gift (11:17). Some think these too were known languages; others ecstatic praise. Its role here is plain: it is the evidence that convinced Peter's companions. Pentecostal teaching takes this verse with 2:4 and 19:6 as showing that tongues are the first outward sign of baptism in the Spirit (Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, 8); most other churches see tongues as one gift among many (1 Corinthians 12:30).

p: The same verb as the eunuch's "What is stopping me" (8:36). Peter turns it into a question no one can answer.
b: Peter's question expects "no": no one can refuse baptism to those God has already given his Spirit. In Jerusalem he will put it more strongly, asking who he was to stop God (11:17). The circumcision of these Gentiles is not raised at all; the question comes back in chapter 15, where Peter recalls this day (15:7–9).
orig: μήτι τὸ ὕδωρ δύναται κωλῦσαί τις (mēti to hydōr dynatai kōlysai tis)
